title: Why Becoming An Expert In Classroom Management Equals Higher Test Scores https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/11/20/classroom-management-and-higher-test-scores/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that strong classroom management is itself an academic intervention, translating directly into higher standardized test scores regardless of a class's roster. He identifies five specific mechanisms: increased time on task from fewer interruptions, sharpened ability to concentrate during independent work, greater attention to detail cultivated through consistently high expectations, stronger habits of following directions built through repeated practice of routines, and higher levels of student trust that make effort and encouragement effective. He frames these as skills that develop gradually through daily classroom experience rather than through direct test-prep instruction, arguing that time spent building management expertise is inherently time spent building academic performance. The piece closes by suggesting that visible test score gains will eventually prompt colleagues and administrators to notice.
points: Classrooms with expert-level management see measurably higher standardized test scores regardless of student roster.
Increased time on task and reduced interruptions can amount to weeks or months of additional effective learning time per year.
Attention to detail and the ability to follow directions are test-taking skills built gradually through classroom routines, not direct instruction.
Student trust in the teacher is a prerequisite for effort and encouragement to translate into better test performance.
Investing in classroom management expertise is framed as, in effect, investing directly in academic outcomes.
quotes: Standardized test scores are noticeably higher, year after year, in classrooms with exceptional classroom management. It doesn’t matter who is on the roster.

Over the course of a school year, the difference in quality learning time between a typical classroom and one taught by a classroom management expert can be staggering—amounting to weeks, even months, more in learning time.
In classrooms with few interruptions, the ability of students to concentrate increases tenfold.
This hyper attention to detail is an important test-taking skill that develops over a period of months and is best learned through experience.
The ability to follow directions is a test-taking skill students learn primarily through the practice and repetition of routines and procedures.

If your students don't like and trust you, your encouragement will fall on deaf ears. If students simply give their best, if they merely test to their ability level, your test scores will be higher than they've ever been.

You’ll experience fewer and fewer of the concerns most teachers carry with them every day, and before long your test scores will take the kind of jump that will get your principal and fellow teachers wondering…
